plan.why: Headlines from Oct 12 (NewsNation, Nautilus) overstate a post hoc marker study. A myth-bust with a list framework fits the carousel quota and the 20% myth slot. | fact-check: The study is real and now peer-reviewed: Corley et al., 'Semaglutide slows epigenetic aging in a randomized trial of HIV-associated lipohypertrophy', Nature Communications, June 2, 2026. It was a post hoc analysis of a 32-week phase 2b RCT (45 semaglutide, 39 placebo) using 17 DNA-methylation clocks. Cite the Nature Communications version, not the 2025 medRxiv preprint. Don't call it 'new'. The results are model estimates adjusted for covariates, so present clock changes as 'estimated' and avoid 'reversed age'. social.facebook_caption:
Does semaglutide (Ozempic) actually slow aging? A new study looked at "epigenetic clocks" — lab tests that estimate biological age from DNA tags — in 84 adults with HIV-associated lipohypertrophy. After 32 weeks, several of 17 clocks estimated slower aging in the semaglutide group than in the placebo group.

Here's the catch: this was a post hoc analysis in one specific group, over 32 weeks. These clocks are markers, not a measure of how long you'll live, and the findings haven't been confirmed in new trials or other populations yet. What we do know, from bigger trials: semaglutide lowered major heart events in adults with heart disease and overweight/obesity without diabetes (SELECT) and lowered kidney-outcome risk in adults with type 2 diabetes and kidney disease (FLOW).

Curious headlines are fun, but context matters. Save this for the next aging headline.

factcheck.summary: The content is accurate, framed with the right caution, and safe. I confirmed S1 exists: Corley et al., "Semaglutide slows epigenetic aging in a randomized trial of HIV-associated lipohypertrophy", Nature Communications, published June 2, 2026, according to the UC San Diego press release. The Nature page itself requires a login, so I checked its details through the indexed article listing, the PMC/medRxiv preprint and the UC San Diego release. They match the slides: a post hoc epigenetic analysis of a 32-week, double-blind, placebo-controlled phase 2b trial, with 45 people on semaglutide and 39 on placebo (84 in the clock analysis, out of 108 in the trial), 17 DNA-methylation clocks, and results adjusted for sex, BMI, hsCRP and sCD163. The 'markers, not lifespan' and 'needs confirmation' framing matches lead author Corley's own caveat: "We are not saying that semaglutide reverses aging." SELECT checks out: 6.5% vs 8.0% had the primary heart outcome, mean follow-up 39.8 months, about a 20% lower relative risk (HR 0.80), in adults with existing heart disease and overweight or obesity, without diabetes. FLOW checks out: 18.7% vs 23.2% on the primary composite, a 24% lower risk, in adults with type 2 diabetes and chronic kidney disease. NEJM blocked direct access to both trial papers, so I confirmed those numbers through secondary summaries. Safety is fine: the protein tip has a kidney-disease caveat, and the prescriber line is there. It gives no dosing and no advice to stop or switch. The minor wording fixes below are optional precision edits.

issues.problem: This leaves out lipohypertrophy, which every participant had. That affects who the result applies to, even among people with HIV. The 'Still unknown' column also says 'not yet tested in RCTs', which is stronger than we can verify.
issues.fix: detail: "84 adults with HIV and belly-fat buildup (lipohypertrophy)"; value: "People without HIV or lipohypertrophy"

issues.problem: The significant changes showed up on several of the 17 clocks, not all of them. The current wording could suggest every clock moved.
issues.fix: detail: "Slower aging estimated on several of 17 clocks"

issues.claim: Effects on lifespan, and in people without HIV, haven't been shown in randomized trials.
issues.problem: This misses the lipohypertrophy population detail. The sentence is accurate but could be tighter.
issues.fix: "Fact: one study estimated slower aging on DNA-methylation clocks in adults with HIV and lipohypertrophy. Those are markers. Effects on lifespan, and in other groups, haven't been shown."
